1. Recap: File Structure at Full Scale
blocks.text: 1. Recap: File Structure at Full Scale

blocks.content: The File Structure topic in the HCL module covered the basics, main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, this topic applies that same convention at the scale of a genuinely complete, real project.
This is deliberately the first topic in the Best Practices module, project structure is often the first real decision a new project actually has to make.
Everything covered here builds directly on modules, state, and backend concepts already understood from earlier in this course.
By the end of this topic, laying out a new, real project should feel like a deliberate, well-informed decision.

2. Root-Level Files
A real project's root level typically holds main.tf for primary resources, variables.tf for inputs, outputs.tf for outputs, and providers.tf for provider configuration.
This is exactly the convention already covered, worth recapping directly here as the genuine foundation everything else in this topic builds on.
Some real teams also add a versions.tf, holding the required_providers and required_version blocks, covered fully in the Version Pinning topic ahead.
This root layer represents the actual root module, recap from the Modules module, the real entry point of the entire project.

blocks.content: 3. A modules/ Directory
Recall the Modules module, real, reusable pieces of configuration typically live in their own modules/ directory, called from the root configuration.
This keeps genuinely reusable logic cleanly separated from the specific, real resources a particular project actually deploys.
Each subdirectory under modules/ is its own, complete child module, exactly the structure already covered in the Module Structure topic.
This separation is what makes real reuse, covered in the Reusable Modules topic, genuinely practical at the project level.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550390965-282797534.png
blocks.alt: Reusable pieces, cleanly separated, recap the Modules module applied here

blocks.content:
.
├── main.tf
└── modules/
    ├── network/
    └── compute/
4. An environments/ Directory
Recall Dev vs Stage vs Production from the Workspaces module, teams choosing the separate-configurations pattern typically organize this as a real environments/ directory.
Each subdirectory represents one genuinely separate, real environment, dev, staging, production, each its own complete root module.
Teams using workspaces instead do not need this directory at all, exactly the tradeoff already covered honestly in that earlier module.
Recognizing which pattern a project uses shapes this entire structural decision from the very start.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550392909-883593314.png
blocks.alt: Recap: separate environments, structured directly as real, honest project layout

blocks.content: 5. Scaling With Project Size
A small, simple project genuinely needs very little structure, root-level files alone are often entirely sufficient.
A genuinely larger, more complex project benefits from the fuller structure covered in this topic, modules/, and possibly environments/, organized deliberately.
Over-structuring a genuinely small project adds real, unnecessary complexity, under-structuring a genuinely large one creates real, growing confusion.
Matching structure to actual, real project size and complexity is the practical judgment this topic builds toward.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784550394868-458940729.png
blocks.alt: A real, practical judgment, matching structure to actual project size

blocks.content: 6. A Real, Complete Example
Bringing this topic's practices together, a genuinely complete real project layout combines root-level files, a modules/ directory, and, where relevant, an environments/ directory.
This is not a rigid, universal template, it is a real, practical starting point, adaptable to a specific, real project's actual needs.
Folder Organization, covered in the next topic, goes further into real, alternative patterns for genuinely larger, more complex projects.
This example is worth treating as a genuine baseline for any new, real Terraform project.

7. A Real, Common Mistake
Everything crammed into one, giant, unwieldy file is a genuinely common, real mistake, especially in a project's earliest, fastest-moving days.
This often happens innocently, adding just one more resource to an already-large main.tf feels easier than restructuring at that specific moment.
The honest fix is splitting files by real, logical concern early, before a project genuinely outgrows a single, unwieldy file.
A file that has grown noticeably large is worth treating as a real, concrete signal that restructuring is genuinely due.

blocks.content: 8. Documenting the Structure
A real README, briefly documenting the structure itself, is a small, genuinely worthwhile habit for anyone joining a real, existing project later.
This mirrors the same documentation habit already covered for modules, secrets, and workspace decisions earlier in this course.
A short, real explanation of what lives where removes a genuine, real barrier for anyone new to a project.
This habit costs very little real, upfront time, and pays back considerably more later.

blocks.content: 9. Migrating an Existing Project's Structure
Restructuring an already-running, real project is genuinely possible, using terraform state mv, recap the State Commands topic, to move resources without destroying them.
This is worth planning deliberately, one real, small step at a time, rather than attempting a single, large, risky restructuring all at once.
Testing a migration against a genuinely disposable, real copy of state first, before touching production, is a worthwhile, honest precaution.
This connects directly back to the state mv real trigger already covered, renaming or moving a resource in code.

10. Onboarding a New Team Member
A well-structured, real project, documented with the README habit covered earlier, is genuinely faster for a new team member to actually understand.
Walking a new, real team member through the structure directly, root files, modules/, and environments/, is a small, worthwhile onboarding step.
This real, practical payoff is often the clearest, most tangible sign that a project's structure was genuinely worth the upfront, deliberate effort.
A structure that requires extensive, real explanation before it makes sense is often a genuine signal the structure itself is not quite right.

blocks.content: 11. Structure and CI/CD
A consistent, real project structure also makes CI/CD pipelines, covered fully in their own module ahead, considerably simpler to write and maintain.
A pipeline can genuinely assume main.tf lives at a predictable, real path, rather than needing special-case logic for every, individually different project.
This is a real, practical payoff worth anticipating now, even before that later module covers CI/CD mechanics in full.
Structure, decided deliberately here, quietly makes several, later real practices genuinely easier throughout the rest of this course.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A real project structure typically combines root-level files, a modules/ directory, and, where relevant, an environments/ directory.
Match structure to actual project size, a small project needs little, a genuinely larger one benefits from this fuller layout.
Split files by logical concern before a project outgrows one, unwieldy file, and document the structure itself in a real README.
